title: Periorbital Peril: Preseptal vs. Orbital Cellulitis
summary: A comprehensive guide to distinguishing and managing infections around the orbit. While preseptal cellulitis is confined to the superficial tissues, orbital cellulitis is a sight- and life-threatening emergency involving the post-septal space.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: The fundamental distinction lies at the **Orbital Septum**, a fibrous layer extending from the orbital periosteum to the tarsal plates. **Preseptal Cellulitis** involves the skin and soft tissues anterior to the septum. **Orbital Cellulitis** involves the orbital contents (fat and extraocular muscles) posterior to the septum, representing a surgical emergency.

sections.title: Microbiology & Pathogens
content: Streptococcus pneumoniae (Most common Gram +)
Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA)
Streptococcus pyogenes
Haemophilus influenzae (Decreased post-vaccine era)
Anaerobes: Bacteroides, Fusobacterium (Associated with dental source)
Fungi: Mucor/Aspergillus (Immunocompromised/Diabetics)

content.explanation: Signs of ORBITAL involvement: P for Proptosis, R for Restriction of motility, O for Optic nerve dysfunction (RAPD/Vision loss), P for Pain on eye movement.

rows: Bilateral signs, CN III, IV, V1, V2, VI palsies.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Full Ocular Exam: Check VA, Pupils, Color Vision, and IOP.
2. Laboratory: CBC with diff, Blood cultures (positive in <10% adults, higher in kids).
3. Imaging: CT Orbit/Sinuses with contrast (Gold Standard). Look for fat stranding, abscess, or sinus opacification.
4. Microbiology: Culture any wound drainage or nasal secretions.
5. Lumbar Puncture: Only if meningeal signs are present.

sections.title: Radiological Red Flags (CT/MRI)
content: Displacement of the globe by a fluid collection (Subperiosteal Abscess)
Gas bubbles within the orbit (Anaerobic infection)
Dilation of the Superior Ophthalmic Vein (CST)
Thickening of the Extraocular Muscles
Intracranial extension (Epidural or Brain abscess)

sections.title: Orbital Management Protocol
content: Step 1: ADMIT to hospital for IV antibiotics and close observation.
Step 2: INITIAL ANTIBIOTICS: Ceftriaxone (2g IV q12h) + Vancomycin (15mg/kg q12h) + Metronidazole (for anaerobes).
Step 3: NASAL DECONGESTANTS: Oxymetazoline spray to facilitate sinus drainage.
Step 4: MONITOR: Vision, pupils, and motility every 4-6 hours.
Step 5: SURGERY: If vision worsens, no improvement in 24-48h, or large abscess present.

sections.title: Surgical Indications
content: Decreasing Visual Acuity or worsening RAPD
Large Subperiosteal Abscess (SPA) >10mm or in older children (>9 yrs)
Abscess of the Frontal Sinus
Failure to respond to IV antibiotics within 48 hours
Evidence of Intracranial Extension
Need for diagnostic biopsy (suspected fungus)

branches: Thyroid Eye Disease (usually bilateral, no fever)

sections.title: Pediatric Pearls
content: Children <9 years often have single-pathogen aerobic infections; respond better to medical therapy.
Children >9 years more likely to have polymicrobial/anaerobic infections and higher surgical rates.
Subperiosteal abscesses can be managed medically in very young kids if vision is stable and abscess is small (<10mm).

sections.title: CST: The Deadly Complication
content: Rapidly progressive bilateral involvement
Multiple Cranial Nerve Palsies (III, IV, VI)
Hypoesthesia in V1/V2 distribution
Severe headache and meningismus
High risk of mortality (30%) and permanent morbidity

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The CT scan must include the sinuses; the ethmoid sinus is the primary source in the majority of cases.
If you can't see the eye due to eyelid swelling, get a CT scan immediately.
Pupillary assessment and color vision (using a red bottle cap) are sensitive markers for early optic nerve compression.
Always check for dental pain or recent dental procedures; these favor anaerobic infections.
A 'quiet' eye with proptosis is unlikely to be cellulitis; think neoplasm or TED.
